name: Curitiba-Afonso Pena International Airport
before:
Curitiba's airport, 18 km south east of downtown in the neighbouring municipality of São José dos Pinhais. It is operated by ASUR, and a shuttle bus and the 208 city bus route both run into the centre.

The terminal is a good one: 45,000 square metres, fourteen jetways and rated for up to 15 million passengers. It opened in 1996, and the terminal it replaced became the cargo building.

One thing to warn clients about. The weather here is unreliable, and winter mornings in particular bring fog and smog that can hold flights. The secondary runway 11/29 is small and its equipment is dated, so there is less flexibility than a two runway layout suggests. The main runway was lengthened in 2008 and there are plans to lift it to Category III instrument approaches.

The airport was built during the Second World War by the Brazilian Air Force with the United States Army, finished in 1945 too late to see much use, and opened to civil traffic in January 1946. It is named after Afonso Pena, the sixth President of Brazil.
after:
Curitiba's airport, 18 km south east of the city centre in the municipality of São José dos Pinhais. It is operated by ASUR, and buses run into the centre.

The terminal has fourteen jetways and is rated for about 15 million passengers a year. It opened in 1996, and the terminal it replaced became the cargo building.

The airport was built during the Second World War by Brazil's Air Ministry with the United States Army and finished in 1945, shortly before the war ended. It opened to civil traffic in January 1946 and is named after Afonso Pena, the sixth President of Brazil.

claims.note: The main airport for Curitiba; Bacacheri (BFH), inside the city, is a small airport run by the same concession company.

claims.note: ASUR, the Mexican airport group, completed its purchase of Motiva's whole airport platform on 1 September 2026 and took over operations that day; the concession company, its staff and its website carry on (the site still shows the Motiva and CCR names, and DECEA's live entry still names 'CCR AEROPORTOS' as the aerodrome's operator). Motiva, the seller, is counted as a separate organisation from ASUR and the airport company ASUR now owns. OurAirports' home link (ccraeroportos.com.br/curitiba-pr) is CCR's old domain; the airport's pages are now at aeroportos.motiva.com.br, which Wikipedia's infobox also gives.

claims.note: Was 'a shuttle bus and the 208 city bus route both run into the centre'. The operator's live transport page lists no airport shuttle and no route 208: it names lines 515 (Terminal Central to the airport) and E32 (airport to Terminal Boqueirão), run by Auto Viação São José dos Pinhais, and its about page says buses are an option for reaching central Curitiba. Curitiba's transport authority (URBS) shows its lines only through a script-driven picker, so the route numbers could not be checked there.

claims.claim: fog and smog on winter mornings hold flights
claims.wasBefore: The weather here is unreliable, and winter mornings in particular bring fog and smog that can hold flights.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone after more than three tries. Bem Paraná answered with Cloudflare's 'Just a moment' check and Aeroin with a 'Javascript is required ... before you are allowed to see this page' gate (neither tried again); Banda B refused the link lister (403); Folha answers 'Blocked by egress policy' (one browser attempt on its old http address was made before that answer was read; the proxy refused it and nothing loaded); the own-site searches of Tribuna do Paraná, G1, CNN Brasil and Agência Brasil returned nothing usable; the operator's FAQ, travel guide and Airport Technology do not mention fog. Worth restoring if a Curitiba news report of fog closures can be read.

claims.claim: secondary runway small with dated equipment
claims.wasBefore: The secondary runway 11/29 is small and its equipment is dated, so there is less flexibility than a two runway layout suggests.
claims.why: 'Dated equipment' rests on Wikipedia alone. For Andy: DECEA's live entry shows runway 11/29 (1,798 m) with non-precision approaches only, against a Category II approach on runway 15 and Category I on 33 of the 2,218 m main runway.

claims.wasBefore: The main runway was lengthened in 2008
claims.why: Wikipedia alone; the operator's history records runway improvements in 2012 but no 2008 lengthening.

claims.wasBefore: there are plans to lift it to Category III instrument approaches
claims.why: Stale: Airport Technology reported a Category III system as part of works due by April 2013, and DECEA's live entry still gives runway 15 Category II (as installed in 2002, operator). No current plan found.
Corrected to Brazil's Air Ministry (the Ministério da Aeronáutica), which the operator and Wikipedia name as the builder.

claims.claim: too late to see much use
claims.wasBefore: too late to see much use
claims.why: Wikipedia alone ('never saw heavy military movement'); softened to finished shortly before the war ended.

Held back: the old text gives no traffic figure, so this replaces nothing. Panrotas (Motiva's 2025 figures, 2 February 2026) gives 6.1 million and Wikipedia's infobox 6,082,222 (+17 per cent). The operator's own January 2026 release says 'cerca de 5 milhões' a year, which looks out of date against its December 2025 month alone (540,916).

TAP's own page lists Curitiba among its destinations. Worth adding for UK agents if Andy agrees.
